nf: Metal detecting is allowed on national forest land, but not at historic or archaeological sites: old homesteads, logging and CCC camps, mills and Native sites more than 100 years old are protected (36 CFR 261.9 and ARPA). Detect the open ground; look only at the old site itself.
bl: Casual metal detecting is generally allowed, but historic and archaeological sites more than 100 years old are protected by ARPA. Look only at the old site itself.
wd: Wisconsin DNR land (state parks, forests, wildlife and fishery areas, natural areas, trails) allows detectors only to find a specific lost item, with a permit from the property office, May 1 to Oct 15 (NR 45.04(3)(i)). Hobby detecting is not allowed: look only.
wcf: County forest rules are set county by county. Some counties sell a detecting permit (Marinette, $5), some ban digging or collecting. Call the county forestry office before you swing.
lp: Local park: the city or county ordinance decides. Many allow detecting, some need a permit (Washington and Dakota counties in Minnesota, beaches only in Dakota) or ban digging in lawns. Check the park rules, plug and fill every hole.
msp: Minnesota state parks allow detectors only to locate a specific lost item, with the park manager's OK (Minn. R. 6100.0900). Hobby detecting is not allowed: look only.
mwma: No detecting rule for WMAs turned up in Minnesota's WMA rules (ch. 6230), so it is not clearly banned, but archaeological sites on state land are protected by the Minnesota Field Archaeology Act. Call the area wildlife office before you dig.
msf: Minnesota state forest or DNR land

No detecting rule for state forests turned up in Minnesota's state forest rules (6100.3000-.4300), so it is not clearly banned, but archaeological sites on state land are protected by the Minnesota Field Archaeology Act. Call the area forestry office before you dig.
misp: Michigan state park or recreation area

Detecting only in the areas the Michigan DNR has designated open (mostly beaches and some day-use areas). Banned at historic and archaeological sites; finds are shown to park staff and artifacts stay where they are.
misf: Michigan state forest or game area
No clear statewide detecting rule turned up for Michigan state forests and game areas. Artifacts on state land belong to the state. Call the DNR field office before you dig.
np: Metal detectors are not allowed on National Park Service land (36 CFR 2.1(a)(7)). Look only.
nw: Metal detecting is not allowed on national wildlife refuges unless the refuge says otherwise. Look only.
tr: Tribal land: detect only with the tribe's written permission.
sna: Scientific and natural areas protect rare ground; nothing may be dug or taken. Look only.
xa: Public land closed to the public
Owned by a public agency but closed to public access. Stay out unless the agency says otherwise.
ng: Owned by a land trust or other private conservation group. Ask the owner; many allow walking but not digging.
os: Owned by another public agency (university, state agency, regional body). Ask the managing agency before you dig.
